title: Fendt, Harrison, Ware, Cardona-Rivera, Roberts, Achieving the Illusion of Agency (ICIDS 2012)
label: research
claim: Three text choose-your-own-adventure versions (branching; non-branching with immediate text feedback; non-branching, no feedback), Stump Junkman story, snowball-sampled online participants. Abstract: 'in most cases no significant difference' in reported agency between branching and linear-with-acknowledgement. But branching beat the no-feedback linear story on every agency question (p=0.05), and beat the feedback version on 'I felt that the story would have been different if I had selected different choices' (p=0.05) and marginally on control (p=0.1). The second hypothesis (feedback story > no-feedback story) was NOT proven: one question only. Authors themselves flag 'psychological priming' from labelling the task a choose-your-own-adventure, and that choices were substantively different (sword vs crossbow). Supports 'acknowledge the choice' as preserving most agency, not all; does NOT show feedback alone suffices without the genre frame.

title: Cardona-Rivera, Robertson, Ware, Harrison, Roberts, Young, Foreseeing Meaningful Choices (AIIDE 2014)
read: full (PDF text-extracted; abstract and related-work section read, limitations skimmed)
label: research
claim: Abstract: 'A choice positively contributes to a player's sense of agency when it leads to meaningfully different content'; n = 88 played a choose-your-own-adventure and 'reported a higher sense of agency when faced with choices that differed in situational content over choices that didn't, despite these choices differing in non-situational ways.' Hypothesis is that the player must FORESEE the options leading to meaningfully different states (perceived, not necessarily actual, difference). Related-work section also notes Fendt's finding that half of six choices rated lower in agency across all treatments (e.g. sword vs crossbow). Does not test a literal 'X will remember that' message.

title: Will Armstrong and Patrick, Do You Copy? Dialog System and Tools in Firewatch (GDC 2017) [02:00]
label: developer
claim: Design origin [02:00-02:59]: the first prototype had Henry driving every conversation, 'interruptible at any time by Henry', so they adopted Valve's bark system; the radio design took its cues from the 2008 Prince of Persia's dedicated button to make the companion talk (hit anytime to have the companion chat about what happened or where you are; auto-caption garbled, paraphrased). The shipped game is 'long conversations with your boss Delilah over a radio' while hiking. Dialogue is triggered by game events (e.g. tossing a beer can) tested against blackboard facts.

title: Will Armstrong and Patrick, Do You Copy? Dialog System and Tools in Firewatch (GDC 2017) [07:00]
label: developer
claim: Memory of choices [07:00]: a global blackboard holds 'anything that we needed to remember from day to day... over the course of the game what you named your dog and systemic things like how long it has been since the last time you decided to have a conversation'. Day-specific blackboards let designers track 'have you left the tower today' without day-one logic leaking into day two.

title: Will Armstrong and Patrick, Do You Copy? Dialog System and Tools in Firewatch (GDC 2017) [08:00]
label: developer
claim: Acknowledgement via state [08:00-13:59]: the turtle gag has 'six turtles in the game' and 'whichever one you see first that's the canonical' one, a late-built workaround for 'nobody never finding one perfect spot'. The caption for the player's choice is picked at the moment the choice is shown by testing requirements ('dog is mayhem'), so the line the player sees names the turtle after the dog they named at the start. Dialogue choices are compiled on demand, not ahead of time.

title: Will Armstrong and Patrick, Do You Copy? Dialog System and Tools in Firewatch (GDC 2017) [18:00]
label: developer
claim: Reactive scenes [18:00-20:59]: the teens scene 'never stopped growing'; 'every time we did a play test someone would want to interact with the teens in a new way and we always wanted to support that'. 'Anything that people tried to do we tried to make work.' The scene reacts to approaching while already on the radio, Delilah overhearing, dialogue choices, silence ('if I'm not gonna say anything'), withdrawing, sneaking past, or throwing their stuff in the lake. Characters keep talking while the player decides what to say.

title: Will Armstrong and Patrick, Do You Copy? Dialog System and Tools in Firewatch (GDC 2017) [22:00]
label: developer
claim: Stall risk, 1 [22:00-24:59]: the teens event graph had 'a red box that's a node you have to hit for the game to essentially continue playing' and 'if you interrupt any one of those chains... you're sort of broken'. Because 'every line is independent could be fired from any way anywhere', context (are the teens aware of me, have I thrown their boom box in the water) 'change the entire shape of the conversation'. Progress-required beats exist inside branching dialogue and a broken chain stalls the game.

title: Will Armstrong and Patrick, Do You Copy? Dialog System and Tools in Firewatch (GDC 2017) [32:00]
label: developer
claim: Pacing/spacing of story talk [33:00-35:00]: the day-two Julia relationship conversation is a four-part chain 'triggered by many areas in the world that you sort of walk through' but 'each one of those doesn't necessarily trigger the same conversation'. It depends on 'how long has it been since the last time you spoke we wanted to space these out' and on what the player has already shared. Same conversation plays very differently if Henry shuts Delilah down [31:00-33:00] versus has shared earlier [32:00-33:00]; Delilah's reaction is the acknowledgement of earlier choices.

title: Will Armstrong and Patrick, Do You Copy? Dialog System and Tools in Firewatch (GDC 2017) [34:00]
label: developer
claim: Selection by specificity [34:00-38:00]: sort event variants by number of requirements and take the first match, 'the most specific thing you could be talking about'. The absence of a fact is valid context: if you've never mentioned a breakup, Delilah 'will assume things about you she'll just start making things up' (projecting a plan to get back with an ex), which 'makes her seem like a very real person and really the player hasn't done anything to earn that'. When she knows more she asks targeted questions to pull the player in. Count-sorting breaks when facts depend on each other, so designers need a priority override [37:00].

title: Will Armstrong and Patrick, Do You Copy? Dialog System and Tools in Firewatch (GDC 2017) [35:00]
label: developer
claim: Disputes 'let the player interrupt anything' [35:00, 37:00-39:00, 47:00-48:00]: they added a 'non interruptible' conversation type for chains 'we just can't let them break because the game state depends on it' (Delilah must learn the truth about the wife). The cost: modal state (radio lock, black bars, music) had to be undone on every exit of a branching conversation, and one added choice could mean 'you can no longer radio about anything ever again in the rest of the game until you load from a save'. Their fix was a debug option to force the radio back on, and in hindsight conversations should be first-class data with the guarantee living on the conversation, not on any single line.

title: Will Armstrong and Patrick, Do You Copy? Dialog System and Tools in Firewatch (GDC 2017) [49:00]
label: developer
claim: Walk-away safety net [49:00, Q&A]: no programmatic guarantee of hitting required nodes ('we had to play test'), but 'we eventually put in a few safeties': once a teens conversation started they spawned a larger volume so that if the player walked away ('you've chosen not to have this conversation') the characters 'yell at you as you flee' and the story still advanced. This covers the case where the player's movement leaves the trigger area.

title: Will Armstrong and Patrick, Do You Copy? Dialog System and Tools in Firewatch (GDC 2017) [55:00]
label: developer
claim: Unreachable lines and QA [55:00-56:00, Q&A]: in early Steam beta a debug mode 'would actually shoot lines that were played to magpie' so they could track lines never played; they 'could actually see like oh crap there's like 20 lines that are unreachable'. Testing was internal playtests with recorded playthroughs and some analytics heat maps ('we didn't make the best use of that'), then Research Center with log files. Also [54:00-55:00]: a map change left lines saying 'go north' where north was no longer north, so text must be revisited when level layout changes. The talk does not quantify how much dialogue players never hear, does not discuss signposting or what testers missed.

title: Greg Kasavin, Breathing Life into Greek Myth: The Dialogue of Hades (GDC 2021) [01:00]
label: developer
claim: Design goal from the start: infuse a die-and-restart roguelike with a continuous narrative, 'every time you died the story would advance. that was kind of the thing that we were excited about early on.' Team stayed small, a little over three years of development, first early access game, first fully voiced game.

title: Greg Kasavin and Darren Korb, Breathing Life into Greek Myth: The Dialogue of Hades (GDC 2021) [04:00]
label: developer
claim: Scale numbers stated: about 30 fully voiced characters, 'over 21 000 voice lines', one minor character has 120 lines, and a roughly 300,000-word total the localization team confirmed. 'We did not realize the scope of the voice over content in this game until we were basically done.' (Also repeated at [51:00] for localizing 'the 300 000 or so words'.)

title: Greg Kasavin, Breathing Life into Greek Myth: The Dialogue of Hades (GDC 2021) [08:00]
label: developer
claim: Why narrative in a roguelike: they wanted the narrative 'to mitigate the kind of sting of failure that can make you want to rage quit out of a roguelike game instead of experiencing what's so great about roguelike games which is that they're different every single time you play.' Voice was the tool, since they lacked motion-captured cutscenes.

title: Greg Kasavin, Breathing Life into Greek Myth: The Dialogue of Hades (GDC 2021) [10:00]
label: developer
claim: Content-volume question they set themselves: 'it's a huge game you can play forever, how many voice lines do you need to support that and to make it really feel like you're not running out of content at any particular point.' The answer turned out to be 21,000+ lines.

title: Greg Kasavin, Breathing Life into Greek Myth: The Dialogue of Hades (GDC 2021) [29:00]
label: developer
claim: Signposting by structure: most characters can simply be skipped ('if you don't like talking to hades you don't like talking to dusa or achilles forget about them you could just walk right by and it's fine') but Megaera, the first boss, 'stands in your way' and is met 'over and over again.' She is the unskippable carrier of the unfolding story, built so the boss relationship 'reflects the player's own journey' (first fight vs the 20th). She ended up with the third most lines in the game ([31:00]).

title: Greg Kasavin, Breathing Life into Greek Myth: The Dialogue of Hades (GDC 2021) [33:00]
label: developer
claim: A play-forever loop that keeps hitting the same characters 'meant that there was no shortage of content ideas.' Frequent recording deadlines tied to early access milestones cured writer procrastination. An early story outline mattered, 'knowing where it was all going', while the day-to-day writing was tactical. Lines were written straight into Google Sheets or game data.

title: Greg Kasavin, Breathing Life into Greek Myth: The Dialogue of Hades (GDC 2021) [34:00]
label: developer
claim: Repetition: heavy emphasis on 'barks', 'quick repeatable lines that mostly zagreus would say in all sorts of different contexts... we didn't want these lines to be repetitive so by the time we play through all the different options it has been hours and hours and hours and you don't notice the repeats.' Script sheet carries line, context and a subtext/sentiment column (what is really behind the line) because the audio director records without the writer.

title: Greg Kasavin, Breathing Life into Greek Myth: The Dialogue of Hades (GDC 2021) [43:00]
label: developer
claim: Sequencing mechanism: story events live as script-like data per NPC (NPCData.lua, line by line, arbitrary presentation). 'Events can have various requirements and that is how we determine the sequencing of events along with some good old-fashioned randomness.' Example requirement: you must have interacted with Thanatos at least once. Events are ordered in the file 'with the more generic more repeatable events down at the bottom', so specific story events sit above generic filler.

title: Greg Kasavin, Breathing Life into Greek Myth: The Dialogue of Hades (GDC 2021) [44:00]
label: developer
claim: Eligibility function started simple (chance to play, e.g. 50/50; 'required text lines' meaning has this story event already occurred, 'a requirement I use very frequently') and grew very specific over development (e.g. a long family of fishing requirements: has fish, fish caught this run, total caught, types). He could add requirements on demand as 'story events where the specificity was needed' appeared, 'we couldn't have imagined we would need all this stuff at the very beginning.'

title: Greg Kasavin, Breathing Life into Greek Myth: The Dialogue of Hades (GDC 2021) [45:00]
label: developer
claim: Bark repetition control: barks take the same requirements as story events (per batch or per line) and use a shuffle-bag. 'All of them will play randomly until the whole table is depleted and then we kind of reload the whole table just to get at the maximum amount of variety and reduce chances of anything playing back to back.' Backed by 'lots and lots' of lines.

title: Greg Kasavin, Breathing Life into Greek Myth: The Dialogue of Hades (GDC 2021) [49:00]
label: developer
claim: Story pacing across releases: because it was early access they 'approached the story like a serial almost like a tv show', early access launch as the pilot and 1.0 as the finale, built out 'update by update until we finally introduced the ending' in the last update before launch. An outline kept the through line while characters (e.g. Alecto, Patroclus, unplanned early on) became significant to the story ([23:00]).

title: Greg Kasavin, Breathing Life into Greek Myth: The Dialogue of Hades (GDC 2021) [50:00]
label: developer
claim: Optional moments matter: 'we'd always try to make time for the small so-called unimportant moments... they're actually some of the most delightful moments in the game even though they're not strictly needed.' Disputes a strict 'cut what isn't needed for the plot' discipline.

title: Greg Kasavin, Breathing Life into Greek Myth: The Dialogue of Hades (GDC 2021) [53:00]
label: developer
claim: Early access made story content instantly canonical: 'as soon as we would put new story stuff into the game it was... instantly canonical', so cutting or rewriting a released character was 'unthinkable.' Contrary to the usual iterate-freely view of early access, it locked narrative content in and made them get it right first time. Early access feedback also protected characters from being cut ([47:00], Korb).

title: Greg Kasavin and Darren Korb, Breathing Life into Greek Myth: The Dialogue of Hades (GDC 2021) [56:00]
label: developer
claim: Self-assessed weakness in sequencing: 'maybe an improved priority system for some of the thornier story events would be good as well. it would save a lot of QA headaches on the back end perhaps and small bugs.' (Speaker not clear from captions; the talk never describes an explicit numeric priority system, only requirements, ordering in the file and randomness.) The narrative volume 'spun out of control to a certain extent' and was held together by QA and early access players ([48:00]).

title: Darren Korb, Breathing Life into Greek Myth: The Dialogue of Hades (GDC 2021) [57:00]
label: developer
claim: Recurring voice-recording sessions (up to three or four per week, [52:00]) 'avoided the crush of stuff at the end' and let new ideas be added; he also says 'we would have ended with a much smaller and worse game' without the early access process ([57:00]-[58:00]). The question they set out to answer was 'can early access work for narrative games.'

title: Iten, Steinemann, Opwis, Choosing to Help Monsters (CHI 2018)
label: research
claim: Two studies, subjective measures only (limitations: 'restriction of measures to only subjective experiences, excluding behavior or attitude change'). STUDY 1 (qualitative, online survey, N=27, 8 female, mean age 24.85; 10 students-for-credit, 11 Facebook, 4 Reddit): participants described a choice they found meaningful; deductive thematic analysis of 27 responses (24 different games) found three themes: consequential ('all but one of the explanations included information on how the choice shaped consequences'), social ('The vast majority' involved a social aspect, nearly all with NPCs not players) and moral ('Most of the choices described contained at least one moral option'; most were moral dilemmas, typically Harm/Care vs Ingroup/Loyalty). Consequential was about the player BELIEVING/knowing the choice shaped consequences: 'the inclusion of a belief that one's choice had consequences appeared as crucial', yet 'unknown long-term consequences seemed to add to the meaningfulness for some participants'. STUDY 2 (experiment, 2x2 between-subjects: choice vs no choice x high- vs low-meaningful; N=192 after excluding 69 of 261, MTurk 165 + Reddit 27; cells 51/50/46/45): one short text story (adventurer, werebear, moth creatures, dragon, magical flower) with ONE choice at the end (pick the flower or not). Choice conditions differed from no-choice only by that one choice; no-choice participants were assigned an outcome yoked to the choice-group distribution. High-meaningful framing added social (werebear friend), moral (save mother with the flower vs save bear friend) and 'clear immediate consequences' (dire long-term: live with having lost mother's last hope or with having left the friend to die); low-meaningful: flower grants strength, werebear leaves earlier, endings 'very similar irrespective of the choice' (decline = find another flower safely). DV appreciation (Oliver & Bartsch, 7-pt, alpha .90), also enjoyment and narrative engagement; covariate care morality (alpha .77). Appreciation means (SD): choice/high 5.43 (1.32), choice/low 4.61 (1.43), no-choice/high 5.05 (1.54), no-choice/low 4.64 (1.64). ANCOVA: main effect meaningfulness F(1,184)=9.59, p=.002, eta2=.044; main effect of CHOICE n.s. F(1,184)=1.42, p=.23, eta2=.006; no interactions significant (p .061-.688). Planned contrasts: choice vs no-choice in high-meaningful t(184)=2.04, p=.042, d=0.30; in low-meaningful t(184)=0.83, p=.407, d=0.12; high-meaningful-choice vs other three t(184)=2.19, p=.03, d=0.32. Enjoyment and narrative engagement: no significant effects of choice or meaningfulness (p .067-.997). Outcome picked had no effect on appreciation (high: 5.25 vs 5.26, p=.976; low: 4.21 vs 4.68, p=.339). Authors: choice 'is not a silver bullet, but may only be effective when the choices the player can make are perceived as meaningful'. DEFINITIONS / consequence nuance: manipulation bundled social+moral+consequences together (independent effect of each 'deserves further research'), so they cannot be separated. In the high-meaningful story a different ending followed each choice (two endings) but 'players could not prevent both deaths'; authors cite Nay & Zagal: 'more important than the outcome of a choice is that the impact of what one has done is felt', and 'what did impact appreciation was the ability to choose'. So 'consequential' = perceived/felt impact plus clear stakes, not necessarily changing the story outcome (Life is Strange: friend dies either way). Caveat: branching was confounded with meaningfulness in study 2 (low condition had near-identical endings). NOTHING on explicit feedback/acknowledgement of choices ('X will remember that'); closest is one BioShock anecdote (saved Little Sisters later leave presents) and P16 'you can't change order later on adds further importance'.
